turns.answer: Python dictionaries locate a key by the value’s hash, so the hash must stay constant for as long as the key lives in the dict. Lists are mutable, meaning their contents – and thus any hash derived from them – could change, so Python marks them as unhashable and raises a TypeError if you try to use one as a key. A tuple is immutable and therefore hashable only when every element inside it is also hashable; if you put a mutable object like a list inside, e.g. (1, [2, 3]), the tuple itself becomes unhashable and cannot be used as a key. If a key could change after insertion, its hash would no longer point to the original slot and look‑ups would fail.

turns.answer: BFS explores a graph level‑by‑level using a queue, while DFS goes as deep as possible along a branch using a stack (or the call stack via recursion). Because BFS visits nodes in order of increasing edge distance, the first time it reaches a target it has followed the shortest‑edge path in an unweighted graph; DFS has no such guarantee. Both algorithms must record which vertices have already been visited so they don’t get stuck in cycles or waste time revisiting the same nodes.
